dailyBrief.text: Solon woke up clear and cold at 39°, but it turns into a sunny, dry Saturday with a high near 65° and no rain — a perfect fall day. Overnight the Brewers edged the Rays 3-2 in World Series Game 1, with Game 2 tonight at 8 PM, while Friday's market drop is still the big money story: the Dow fell 653 points as oil spiked. Today is packed close to home: Barack Obama rallies in Cleveland for Sherrod Brown and Amy Acton, the Solon library hosts a hands-on chemistry morning for kids at 10:30, the City of Solon Trick-or-Treat Trail runs 4–6 PM, and the Cavs play their home opener against Brooklyn at Rocket Arena at 7:30 PM.

weekBrief.text: It's a golden fall week ahead in Solon: mostly sunny and dry, highs in the mid-60s warming to the low 70s by Thursday, lows in the 40s, and no real rain in the forecast until late next weekend. The weekend is full — the Cavs' home opener tonight and the Browns at Tennessee on Sunday, the North Union Farmers Market season finale in Chagrin Falls on Sunday morning, and the Cavs back home against Minnesota on Monday — and Halloween lands next Saturday with Ohio State at USC that night. The standout deal is still Miles Farmers Market's jumbo eggs at $1.00 a dozen, good through Tuesday. And with the baby due in early November, this week is for finishing touches and enjoying the calm.

Ukraine says Starlink service is finally back to full speed on Saturday
items.summary:
Ukraine's defence ministry said on Saturday that Starlink and its military version, Starshield, were again working at the speeds the country had before restrictions were imposed more than a week ago. Defence Minister Yevheniy Khmara said monitoring systems were recording a stable connection above 400 km/h, and President Volodymyr Zelensky later confirmed the restoration the same day.

The confirmation matters because it reverses what Ukrainian officials were still saying on Friday evening — that the limits were in place and were disrupting operations. One source in the Donetsk region told CNN on Saturday morning that speeds there were still capped at about 160 km/h, so it is not yet clear the fix has reached every part of the front at once. Zelensky described the service as crucial for frontline logistics and for defending against jet-propelled Shahed drones, which Ukrainian officials say the caps made harder to intercept.

The episode has also left a political dispute unresolved. CNN reported that President Trump asked Elon Musk in a recent phone call to restore full access, while Trump declined to say who made the call and said only that Musk "put it back." Trump and Musk have each denied ordering the original slowdown, and Zelensky separately complained on Friday that promised Patriot interceptors were still delayed.

Watch whether Ukrainian units report the higher speeds holding across regions in the coming days, and whether Washington and Kyiv give a consistent account of who imposed the limits in the first place.

items.title: Ukraine says it hit a major Russian petrochemical plant in Togliatti
items.summary:
Ukrainian forces struck industrial sites in the Russian city of Togliatti on Saturday, according to both sides. The city's mayor, Ilya Sukhikh, said several industrial facilities were damaged and reported no deaths or injuries in early accounts, without naming the sites hit.

Ukraine's General Staff said its target was the Togliattikauchuk petrochemical plant, described as one of Russia's largest makers of synthetic rubber. Kyiv also said it struck the Proton electronics plant in the Oryol region, which it says makes components for cruise and ballistic missiles, and hit an aircraft at the Yeysk airfield in southern Russia, where local authorities acknowledged an attack but reported only minor damage to two apartment buildings.

The strikes are part of Ukraine's campaign against industrial and military targets deep inside Russia, even as Moscow reports shooting down huge numbers of incoming weapons. Russia's Defence Ministry said its air defences destroyed 1,297 drones, one French-made SCALP cruise missile and four Ukrainian Neptune missiles in the previous 24 hours. Oryol's governor also said three people were killed on Friday in a Ukrainian missile strike on an unspecified civilian facility in that region.

Watch for verified damage assessments from Togliatti and Oryol, which will show whether the petrochemical and electronics plants were knocked out of production or only lightly damaged.

items.title: About 1,200 Palestinians forced from their homes as Israel opens a large operation in Hebron
items.summary:
Israel's military forced roughly 1,200 Palestinians to leave their homes in Hebron in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, a Palestinian official told Reuters, as a large operation began a day after two Israeli soldiers were killed at a checkpoint near the city. Hebron's municipal head, Yousef Zouhair Al-Jabari, said about 1,300 more people faced losing their homes on top of those already displaced.

The military said the operation in the Al-Jaladah and Ein Deir Baha neighbourhoods near the checkpoint was aimed at finding militants and weapons, and that demolitions would be carried out. The Palestinian Authority called the operation collective punishment, residents said many people with no connection to the attackers were expelled, and the Palestinian Prisoners' Club said about 70 Palestinians were arrested on Friday and Saturday — a figure Israeli officials had not commented on.

The timing is politically charged. Al-Jabari argued the operation was meant to win settler votes ahead of Israel's parliamentary election on Tuesday, when opinion polls suggest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing coalition could lose its majority. Reuters also reported closures blocking entrances to most West Bank cities and towns, with one father saying he could not get his daughter to Jerusalem for cancer treatment.

This is a material escalation of Friday's checkpoint attack story, not a repeat of it: the question now is how long the displaced families are kept out, how much is demolished, and whether the operation expands in the final days before the vote.

items.title: Typhoon Champi sweeps past Taiwan, leaving 1 dead and 527 injured
items.summary:
Typhoon Champi brushed Taiwan's northeastern coast early on Saturday, killing one person and injuring 527, the island's fire department said. The person who died was a man swept away by waves off Liuqiu Island. At its peak Champi was a super typhoon and one of the strongest Pacific storms this year, and gusts still reached 227 kph in some coastal areas as it passed.

The storm knocked down trees and power lines and sent roof tiles flying, especially around Yilan County, where its centre made a rare loop offshore around midnight before turning north. More than 288,000 homes lost electricity, though most had been reconnected, and the transport ministry reported 259 flights cancelled on Saturday — down from almost 1,000 on Friday. Governments across northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, kept offices and schools closed for a second day.

Champi is now weakening and heading north along the Chinese coast, without an expected landfall there, before moving toward southern Japan. China sent an emergency team to Zhejiang province, readied rescue workers and firefighters, brought thousands of fishing boats back to harbour and evacuated more than 2,000 island visitors.

Watch the damage assessments in Yilan and the storm's effects in Zhejiang through Sunday, when strong wind and heavy rain are still expected on the Chinese coast.

items.title: Magnitude 6.9 earthquake hits off Vanuatu, and the tsunami threat passes
items.summary:
A magnitude 6.9 earthquake struck off Vanuatu in the South Pacific on Saturday at 02:31 GMT, about 197 kilometres west-northwest of Port-Olry at a shallow depth of about 10 kilometres, the U.S. Geological Survey reported. The agency first put the size at 7.2 before revising it down to 6.9. There were no immediate reports of damage or casualties.

A second quake of magnitude 6.3 followed only about four minutes later, roughly 170 kilometres northwest of Port-Olry, also at about 10 kilometres deep. The USGS gave that second event a green alert, signalling a low likelihood of major casualties or damage.

The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center first warned of a possible tsunami threat for the surrounding region, then said in a bulletin at 03:28 GMT that the threat had passed. It cautioned that minor sea-level changes could still occur near the epicentre for several hours, but that no further action was needed beyond normal care near the sea.

Vanuatu sits in one of the world's most earthquake-prone zones, so officials will be watching for aftershocks and for reports from remote islands near Espiritu Santo that can take time to reach the capital.

items.title: Hurricane Vance, a Category 2 storm, churns toward Mexico's Pacific coast
items.summary:
Hurricane Vance rapidly strengthened into a Category 2 storm as it moved toward Mexico's Pacific coast, the National Hurricane Center said, with maximum sustained winds of 110 mph while it was about 385 miles south-southwest of Acapulco. The centre said Vance was nearing major-hurricane strength, though gradual weakening was expected to begin by Saturday.

Even offshore, the storm was already sending gale-force winds and rough seas into Mexico's Gulf of Tehuantepec through its outer bands. Its slow movement adds uncertainty to where it will be in the days ahead and how close it will come to the coast.

Vance is part of an unusually busy Pacific season shaped by El Niño conditions. If it reached major-hurricane status it would be the seventh major hurricane in a row this year in the Pacific, after Nolo, Odalys, Polo, Rachel, Simon and Trudy, according to the AP report.

Watch the next hurricane centre advisories for whether Vance briefly reaches Category 3, where its track bends, and whether watches are posted for communities along the Mexican coast.

items.title: Corruption and "grift" jump to the top of voter worries in the final days before the midterms
items.summary:
Government corruption has climbed to the top of voter concerns less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms, the Wall Street Journal reported, with a Fox News poll published last week ranking it above inflation and gasoline prices. In that poll 88% of voters said they were concerned about corruption in government and 60% said they were extremely concerned.

The shift follows a string of headlines involving people around President Trump. The Journal listed, among others, his ambassador to Greece resigning after an accusation of soliciting $100,000 from a donor, a proposed $50 million deal involving the family of a Venezuelan banker seeking a pardon and the president's former personal lawyer, a Russian businessman funding a wedding afterparty for one of Trump's sons, and two top political advisers consulting abroad for a Russia-aligned government. Trump on Thursday warned his own allies to be honest or face prosecution, in response to a question about a Justice Department inquiry involving longtime adviser Corey Lewandowski.

Democrats have made the issue central, spending $182 million this year on corruption-related ads in House and Senate races — more than the previous four cycles combined, according to AdImpact — and promising investigations if they win a majority. They point to Trump's wealth growth in office, including $1.4 billion last year from crypto ventures by the Journal's account, the gifted Qatari jet, and the pardon of Binance founder Changpeng Zhao.

Republican pollster Whit Ayres told the Journal concern about corruption is higher than he can remember, including among independents and some Republicans, while Trump pollster John McLaughlin argued undecided voters are still deciding mainly on their pocketbooks. Whether corruption or prices moves the last undecided voters is now a central question of the closing stretch.

items.title: Trump's rally blitz is playing defence in Republican country, Reuters finds
items.summary:
President Trump is holding near-daily rallies to turn out Republican voters before the November 3 midterms, but Reuters' review of the tour on Saturday found his travel map looks defensive: twice to Texas, plus Kansas, Ohio, Alaska, Iowa, Montana and South Carolina, with Mississippi planned for Monday and Michigan for Sunday. Those are places Republicans normally win without this kind of effort in the final weeks.

The races explain the map. In Texas, Republican Ken Paxton narrowly trails Democrat James Talarico in polls; in Kansas, incumbent Roger Marshall faces a serious challenge in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century; in Ohio, Jon Husted trails former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown; and in Iowa, Ashley Hinson is in a close race with Josh Turek. Reuters also noted Trump's approval rating at 31% in a Reuters/Ipsos poll released Monday, described as the lowest of either of his terms.

His economic pitch is running into voter reality at the same events. Trump points to low unemployment, record stock prices and a record-low poverty rate, while voters outside a Kansas rally complained about gas and grocery prices. Consumer prices accelerated in September as gasoline surged, and AAA put the national average at $4.27 a gallon, nearly 40% higher than a year ago — a cost Trump says will fall once the Iran war ends.

Reuters also noted uneven crowds behind Trump's boasts about overflow audiences, and a stump turn toward France's unrest as a warning about a Democratic win. For Republican candidates, the test is whether the enthusiasm at these rallies converts into votes for people other than Trump himself, since he is not on the ballot.

items.title: Kamala Harris returns to the campaign trail, with 2028 questions following her
items.summary:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris is back on the campaign trail for Democrats in tight midterm races, Reuters reported on Saturday, after making relatively few public appearances this year. Her tour includes Georgia, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire and Wisconsin as Democrats try to break Republican control of Congress on November 3.

She opened in Las Vegas on Tuesday speaking to Culinary Workers Union members alongside Nevada gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford, attacking what she called the cruelty and corruption of the Trump administration. The next day in Columbus, Mississippi, she campaigned for Scott Colom, who is trying to become the first Democratic senator elected in Mississippi since 1982 in an unusually tight race against Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Harris is a polarising closer. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in June found 39% of Americans viewed her favourably, including 82% of Democrats but only 7% of Republicans and 33% of independents. Strategists quoted by Reuters said parties bring out their heavy hitters at the end of a campaign, and that disillusioned 2024 voters who stayed home may see her differently this time.

Asked recently whether she will run again in 2028, Harris laughed and said she has not decided, adding that the midterms come first. A third White House bid would make her one of the biggest names in a crowded Democratic field, but it would also reopen the chaotic 2024 handover from Joe Biden, which she called reckless in her memoir "107 Days."

items.title: Justice Department tells California counties to set aside ballots from suspected noncitizens
items.summary:
The Justice Department on Friday ordered California county election officials to work with federal agencies to identify suspected noncitizens on their voter rolls and set aside those voters' mail-in ballots, CNN reported on Saturday. A letter from First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli warned that officials who knowingly count ballots cast by noncitizens risk being treated as aiders and abettors to a federal crime.

The order escalates an October fight over a federal list. On October 13 the acting deputy attorney general gave Los Angeles County and California's secretary of state 48 hours to review names sent on a password-protected thumb drive, and the Justice Department last week sued California and Los Angeles County over more than 20,000 mail ballots it associates with likely noncitizens. On Friday it also asked the 9th Circuit to intervene ahead of a hearing scheduled for next week.

California officials are pushing back on the reliability of the federal data. Los Angeles County's clerk said eligibility changes must rest on verifiable information, not unconfirmed matching, and Senator Alex Padilla called the administration afraid and desperate and said it has no authority to interfere. CNN noted that in Nevada, Homeland Security first flagged 15,900 possible noncitizen registrants, confirmed only 185 on manual review, and Nevada officials later said all 185 were U.S. citizens — a conclusion the federal agency disputes.

With ballots already being cast, watch the 9th Circuit and next week's hearing: they will decide whether counties must segregate these ballots while the underlying citizenship claims are tested.

items.title: In Michigan's Senate race, Detroit voters divided over Israel say costs come first
items.summary:
Detroit voters who disagree sharply over Israel and the Democratic Senate nominee are converging on one issue — the cost of living — Reuters reported on Saturday from Michigan. The race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and former Republican congressman Mike Rogers could help decide Senate control, and a RealClearPolitics average puts El-Sayed ahead by two points, 48% to 46%.

Reuters interviewed voters like Dayna Broadnax, a 42-year-old Lyft driver and mother of four, who said gas can take $50 of the $150 she makes on a typical day and that she sometimes skips meals so her children can eat. She said she has not decided, and will back whichever candidate focuses most on lowering costs. A Wayne State senior in Dearborn made a similar point: she supports El-Sayed's stance on funding for Israel, but fears about jobs, rent and groceries weigh more.

El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim U.S. senator, faces real resistance inside the usual Democratic coalition. Some Jewish voters remain angry over his "hurt people hurt people" response to a March attack in which a man rammed a truck into a suburban synagogue while more than 100 children were inside, a comment he later apologised for, and over his brief campaigning with streamer Hasan Piker. A Michigan State professor quoted by Reuters said El-Sayed must win over voters who dislike Trump but have personal or policy reservations about him — and get them to vote at all, rather than sit the race out.

That turnout question is the stakes in miniature: if cost pressure brings uneasy Democrats out despite their reservations, El-Sayed's narrow lead can hold; if they stay home, a seat Democrats need becomes much harder to keep.

items.title: Trump says he may move the press corps out of the White House briefing room
items.summary:
President Trump suggested on Saturday that he may move journalists out of the White House press briefing room, posting on Truth Social that he "may move the Fake News to a less obnoxious location." The room has housed the White House press corps for more than five decades.

The post followed an October 20 New York Times report that Trump told then-press secretary Karoline Leavitt in August to move reporters out of the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room, and told aides the space could again hold the indoor therapy pool installed under Franklin D. Roosevelt and replaced by the briefing room under Nixon. Trump denied that part directly, saying the old pool will never be brought back and that he never thought of doing it. USA Today noted there is currently no press secretary, after Leavitt's departure and Katie Zacharia's five-day tenure earlier this month.

No move has been put into action, and the idea sits inside a longer legal fight over press access. In September Trump sought to bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico, and a federal judge on October 13 ordered the White House to keep allowing those outlets' reporters access, a ruling the administration is contesting. An earlier ban on the Associated Press in February 2025 was also lifted by a federal judge that April.

Watch whether this stays a social-media threat or becomes a formal relocation order — and, if it does, whether courts treat moving the whole press corps differently from the outlet-specific bans judges have already blocked.

items.title: Chinese AI firm Moonshot deliberately weakens hacking skills in its newest model
items.summary:
Beijing-based Moonshot AI said Saturday it trimmed the cyber-offensive abilities of its newest system, Kimi K3.1 Pro, before releasing it. The company describes the model as its most capable in the 3-trillion-parameter class and plans to publish its weights, the files that let outside developers run and modify it, by November 4.

Moonshot said it removed cyber-related material from the training data and from the reinforcement-learning settings used to build the model, while keeping general coding ability. On its own internal test for finding and exploiting software flaws, the safeguarded version scored 81.0%, compared with 90.5% for a version built without those steps. Those results have not been independently verified. The model also offers a 1-million-token context window, and a separate high-speed version is said to run two to three times faster.

The move reflects wider worry that AI systems able to write code, use tools and carry out long multi-step tasks could make sophisticated hacking cheaper and easier. China proposed export controls last week that would ban exports of AI-driven malware-generation technology and restrict tools that help discover vulnerabilities, citing risks to critical infrastructure, defence and government systems.

Because Kimi is open-weight, once the files are widely shared the developer has far less ability to monitor use or update safeguards than with a hosted service. The test ahead is whether other open-model makers follow the same approach.

items.title: Small businesses are using AI widely, but few have built it into their core work
items.summary:
A Goldman Sachs survey of more than 2,400 graduates of its 10,000 Small Businesses programme found 86% now use AI in their business, up from 56% in 2024. Only 15% said AI is fully integrated into their core operations, and more than three-quarters said they could use more training and resources.

To close that gap, Goldman is putting $500 million behind the next chapter of the programme and launching a Small Business AI Institute. It is working with Anthropic, Google, Meta and OpenAI on applied training, workshops for alumni, research on small-business AI use, and efforts to expand access to capital. Plans include a learning series with Anthropic, Google certificate training for nearly 20,000 owners and employees, Meta support through Muse for Small Business, and OpenAI workshops with community-college partners.

Goldman says the programme, launched in 2010, has served nearly 20,000 entrepreneurs across all 50 states and four U.S. territories, representing more than $32 billion in annual revenue and over 350,000 jobs. The new commitment aims to deliver education, capital access and support services to another 10,000 businesses.

The stakes are practical rather than theoretical: if most owners are experimenting with AI but not yet changing how the business actually runs, training and workflow help may matter more than access to another tool. Watch whether follow-up surveys show the share with full integration rising from that 15% base.

items.title: Axios bets AI support for local reporters and paid news feeds will grow the company
items.summary:
Axios chief executive Jim VandeHei laid out a strategy on October 24 that pairs human local reporting with AI support systems. The plan also includes new coverage aimed at executives, paid news feeds for businesses, and more in-person events.

Axios says its local operation already has more than 100 journalists. The idea described in the essay is to use automation to stretch what those reporters can cover, while selling verified reporting both to readers and to AI companies that want reliable news feeds for their own products.

That is a different business model from simply licensing archives. If Axios can package live, verified local reporting as a data product, it creates a revenue line tied directly to demand from large language model firms, while also trying to make expansion into more communities financially sustainable.

The test is whether the added automation and feed revenue actually support wider coverage without hollowing out the reporting itself. No timetable or pricing for the feeds was detailed in the summary published Saturday morning.

items.title: Billionaires seed children's investment accounts through the Trump Accounts programme
items.summary:
Elon Musk this week pledged to give millions of American children individual shares in SpaceX, worth roughly $150 each, through the Trump Accounts programme. He joins Michael and Susan Dell, Ray Dalio and others who are putting money or stock into the government-backed accounts for children.

The programme lets anyone deposit money into an IRA-style account for someone under 18. Babies born from 2025 through 2028 receive an automatic $1,000 deposit, and holders cannot access the money until they turn 18. The Dells' donation is described as $250 for 25 million accounts, focused on children under 10 in lower-income ZIP codes. A White House spokesman said nearly 70 million Trump Accounts have been created.

Investor Brad Gerstner, who conceived the idea six years ago and sold it to the White House, frames it as a new social contract built on broad ownership, comparing its ambition to Social Security's role at the end of life. Critics quoted in the Journal question the timing just before the midterms, the political benefit to donors and to the president, and the tax advantages that can come with donating appreciated shares instead of selling them.

For families, the long horizon is the point: at historic average returns, that initial $1,000 could grow to more than $5,800 in nominal terms over 18 years. What to watch is whether Musk details when and how the SpaceX shares will actually be distributed, since he has not yet done so beyond his public comments.

items.title: Indonesia cuts gas exports to Singapore by about 9% to keep power at home
items.summary:
Indonesia reduced its pipeline natural gas exports to Singapore starting Saturday by 31 million standard cubic feet per day, its upstream regulator SKK Migas said. That amounts to about 9% of the pipeline supply Singapore receives from Indonesia.

The cut is split between sources: 15 million cubic feet per day less from Natuna and another 16 million from Sumatra, according to SKK Migas chairman Djoko Siswanto. The gas is being redirected to meet electricity needs in Batam, Bintan and Sumatra.

The decision follows a blackout earlier this month that lasted 16 hours in Batam and several cities in Indonesia's Riau Islands province. Energy Minister Bahlil Lahadalia said earlier this week he would prioritise domestic use of natural resources and review contracts to protect energy security.

Singapore is exposed because it generates up to 95% of its electricity from natural gas, and most of its Indonesian supply arrives by pipeline. Watch for any Singapore response on replacement supply, and whether Jakarta extends the diversion beyond an initial short-term fix.

items.title: Early voting opens in New York City, with Mayor Mamdani casting his ballot Saturday morning
items.summary:
Early voting began Saturday in New York, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani voted around 10 a.m. at the Metropolitan Museum of Art polling site on the Upper East Side. He said he voted for Governor Kathy Hochul on the Working Families Party line and is campaigning for her re-election against Republican Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman.

Mamdani brought donuts for poll workers and joked afterwards about how quick the process was, saying he voted in about five minutes. Video posted from the site also showed one voter heckling him as he arrived.

Early voting in the city runs through November 1, mostly from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., with longer hours on October 27 and 28 and different hours on October 29. Election Day polls on November 3 are open from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m. Beyond governor, New Yorkers are voting for attorney general, comptroller, congressional and state legislative seats, and five ballot questions backed by the Mamdani administration.

Saturday was also the first statewide early in-person voting day in other states, including Michigan, where the period runs through November 1 for the November 3 general election. Turnout over this first weekend will be an early signal of enthusiasm heading into the final week.

items.title: Judge blocks Homeland Security election-related home visits in nine states
items.summary:
A federal judge has issued a preliminary injunction barring the Department of Homeland Security from conducting election-related field operations that could sweep up U.S. citizens in nine states until polls close on Election Day. The states are Nevada, California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.

Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, acted Wednesday after plaintiffs alleged Homeland Security was sending armed agents to homes to question residents about voter status. She wrote that the evidence created an objectively reasonable fear of law-enforcement entanglements that could intimidate citizens from helping others vote. She paused the order until Friday, giving the administration time to appeal.

The ruling is a setback for the administration's fall campaign against noncitizen voting. Separately, the Justice Department is suing California over roughly 20,000 voters the federal government says it suspects are noncitizens. Homeland Security said Thursday it has no plans to question or investigate people it believes to be U.S. citizens, and Justice Department lawyers argued the government has authority to investigate potential noncitizen voting.

The lawsuit was filed by San Francisco, Santa Clara, the California Nurses Association, National Nurses United and the Voto Latino Foundation. Watch for an appeal in the coming days, which could change what agents may do in the final stretch before November 3.

items.title: Two former FBI officials charged with lying to Congress about the Hunter Biden probe
items.summary:
The Justice Department has charged two former FBI employees, Nikki Floris, 46, and Bradley Benavides, 56, each with one count of making false statements. They made their first court appearances on Friday, and FBI Director Kash Patel announced the arrests.

Prosecutors allege the pair lied in 2023 testimony to a Republican-led congressional investigation, playing down their roles in investigating Hunter Biden and his laptop despite communications, witness accounts and other evidence. According to the complaint described in court, Floris said she had no involvement while prosecutors say she communicated frequently with the case team and helped coordinate responses to news articles about the laptop in real time. Benavides is alleged to have said he learned the FBI had the laptop from Wikipedia in 2023, despite regularly discussing it ahead of the 2020 election.

Both defendants served on the FBI's foreign-influence task force, set up after Russian interference in the 2016 race and disbanded in early 2025. Lawyers for Floris called the charges an attempt to push a false narrative for political points, and Benavides's team called them baseless. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui noted the alleged conduct was several years old and questioned the use of a criminal complaint rather than a grand-jury indictment, pressing for a prompt hearing.

The case lands less than two weeks before Election Day and adds to scrutiny of how the Justice Department is handling politically sensitive cases. The charges themselves have not been proven, and the next hearing is expected to test the government's evidence quickly.

items.title: Skye Blakely adds two more medals at gymnastics worlds, with Simone Biles watching
items.summary:
American gymnast Skye Blakely won bronze medals in both the vault and uneven bars finals on Saturday in Rotterdam, adding to the all-around gold and team silver she had already earned at these world championships. That makes four medals in four events so far, with the balance beam final still to come on Sunday.

In vault, Brazil's Rebeca Andrade won gold with 14.466, ahead of American Claire Pease at silver and Blakely in third. On bars, Blakely scored 14.6 and held on for bronze after France's Elena Colas made mistakes including a large step on her dismount. Algeria's Kaylia Nemour led the bars field with 15.333.

The U.S. men also had a breakthrough: Fred Richard won gold on floor exercise with 14.633, edging defending champion Jake Jarman by just 0.033. Richard is the first American man to win a world floor title since Paul Hamm in 2003. Patrick Hoopes finished off the podium on pommel horse.

Simone Biles attended the finals in the arena and said in an in-arena interview that the atmosphere made her feel as if she were competing herself, praising Blakely's comeback. Blakely's run is especially notable after injury setbacks that derailed earlier Olympic bids, and it positions her strongly as the sport turns toward the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.

items.title: Rabbi attacked with a syringe in Midtown returns to the same street the next day
items.summary:
A 26-year-old rabbi identified only as Yosef returned to West 47th Street in Manhattan's Diamond District the day after he was attacked, resuming the outreach work he has done there four days a week for the past three years. He told the Post on Friday he was shaken but determined not to be intimidated.

Video described in the report shows Yosef, dressed in traditional Orthodox clothing, being followed around 5:30 p.m. Wednesday by a Russian-speaking woman on the busy street. He felt a sharp, needle-like prick in his lower right back near a grocery store, was taken to Bellevue Hospital with his shirt soaked in blood, and was released after roughly three hours.

Yosef said he had never met the woman, that she passed other people, and that he believes he was targeted because he is visibly Jewish. The NYPD Hate Crime Task Force is investigating, and the attacker has not been caught.

He said he decided as he left the hospital that he would go back the next morning, drawing strength from his grandparents, who survived the Holocaust and then built a Jewish home. His return surprised people he visited on 47th Street, and police are still seeking the woman seen in the video.

items.title: Ramaswamy digs in on the Acton mother ad as Trump urges him to keep it running
items.summary:
Republican nominee for Ohio governor Vivek Ramaswamy spent Friday on his party's bus tour, including a stop in Strongsville in suburban Cleveland, refusing to pull a $4 million ad that features his Democratic opponent Amy Acton's estranged mother calling her daughter a liar. President Donald Trump weighed in again on Friday, saying that even knowing Acton's history, Ramaswamy should keep the ad on the air.

The history is why the ad has split Republicans. Acton has said she has not seen her mother since she was 12, when her mother lost custody of her children and her stepfather was indicted by a grand jury on charges of sexually abusing her. Outgoing Republican Gov. Mike DeWine, whom Ramaswamy is running to replace, told reporters Thursday the ad was deeply troubling on its face and worse once the backstory is known. Ramaswamy told reporters Friday the ad had nothing to do with childhood abuse and said voters should hear the mother's claims and decide for themselves, while Vice President JD Vance has also defended him.

CNN's conversations with voters over three days found the party's base largely staying with Ramaswamy, while some moderate and independent voters said the ad changed how they see him — one Madeira independent called it heinous and said it showed a judgment of character she does not want in politics, while other Republicans at the Strongsville stop said they disliked the ad but would still vote for him.

That split is the stakes ten days before the Nov. 3 election, in a state Trump carried by 11 points in 2024. The ad first surfaced Monday night via Ohio blogger D.J. Byrnes, and Ramaswamy's campaign confirmed Tuesday it was theirs and committed $4 million to run it. Watch whether the ad stays up through the final week and whether late polling in the governor's race moves after the bus tour.

items.title: Dover mourns a second teen lost in six weeks as ICE reports unsettle Tuscarawas County's Hispanic community
items.summary:
Dover High School student Julio Habraham Raymundo Ramos, 15, died by suicide on Oct. 20, the school announced to families. It is the second Dover student suicide in about six weeks — freshman Nathan M. Beachy, also 15, died on Sept. 15 — and Superintendent Karie McCrate wrote on Oct. 22 that the district had faced overwhelming loss and would hold small-group forums so families can learn about support programs and share ideas.

Julio's death comes as Tuscarawas County's growing Hispanic community is on edge over reported immigration enforcement. A local Spanish-language community page reported ICE detentions outside a store in Dover and New Philadelphia on Oct. 17, with further monitoring posts on Oct. 20 and Oct. 23; the Beacon Journal could not independently verify a local group's report that three people of Maya descent were detained, and ICE did not reply to questions about its activity in the county. Community posts informed by the family and others said racist bullying at school — mocking accents and using slurs — compounded by the ICE activity weighed on Julio. The priest who will celebrate his funeral Mass on Oct. 31 said he does not believe the ICE activity or harassment directly led to the suicide, and urged mercy for people in need.

Julio was born in Nebaj, Guatemala, came to the United States after age 12, and will be laid to rest in Guatemala, according to his obituary. His family joined a Hispanic community that grew from under 1,000 people in Tuscarawas County in 2010 to roughly 4,400 in 2024. Residents interviewed Oct. 23 described being afraid to go outside and changing daily routines, while also describing the community as hard-working and welcoming.

For Dover, the immediate question is support: counselors, the planned family forums, and how a small district cares for students after two losses in one fall. If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 in the U.S. to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

items.title: Ohio State faculty say the Chase Center's structure threatens academic freedom; center faculty say it does not
items.summary:
At Ohio State's University Senate meeting on Oct. 22, the Committee on Academic Freedom and Responsibility presented a report saying the mandate of the Salmon P. Chase Center for Civics, Culture & Society poses a credible threat to academic freedom. The Senate voted to send the report to its steering committee for further discussion, with Chase Center representation added.

The Chase Center is one of five independent academic centers the Ohio General Assembly required in 2023 at five public universities. At Ohio State it sits in the John Glenn College of Public Affairs and can hire 15 tenure-track faculty whose appointments are held inside the center. The committee's concern is structural, not personal: the law gives the center's director oversight to develop and approve its curriculum, which the report says could let one person decide what is and is not taught, and it describes the center as created with an ideological mission by legislation that received votes from only one party. The committee stressed its concerns are about the powers given to the director, not about current director Lee Strang.

Chase Center professor Michael Clune answered for the center's faculty at the meeting, saying they have not experienced any loss of academic freedom and that the committee's description is wrong in every respect. He noted the director answers to the provost, president and board of trustees, and that the committee did not consult Chase Center faculty about their experiences before writing the report.

The debate is not happening in a vacuum. A Statehouse bill introduced in June by Sen. Jerry Cirino, Senate Bill 461, would entrench the five centers' independence and funding, give directors sole authority over hiring, promotion, tenure and curriculum, and elevate the Ohio State and Toledo directors to deans by Jan. 1. Watch how the Senate steering committee handles the report and how SB 461 moves.

items.title: Ohio early in-person voting is running nearly four times higher than in 2022, while mail requests fall
items.summary:
Ohioans are voting early in person at a pace far above the last midterm. In the first week of early voting, 194,841 Ohioans cast a ballot in person, nearly four times the 50,368 cast at the same point in 2022, and counties had already tallied about a third of their entire 2022 early in-person total. Cuyahoga, Lucas, Lorain and Summit counties — the Cleveland, Toledo and Akron metro areas — had each already cleared 40 percent of their 2022 early vote totals. Today, Saturday Oct. 24, is the first Saturday of early voting in Ohio.

The other side of the shift is mail. Only about 631,079 Ohio voters had requested a mail ballot, down by almost a quarter-million from 2022, continuing a multi-cycle move away from voting by mail. Signal Ohio's county analysis found the same pattern earlier in the cycle: mail requests down 26 percent statewide, with Cuyahoga County down 16.7 percent — tied for the smallest drop in the state — and early in-person voting in Cuyahoga on day one at 1,908 people, up from 547 four years earlier.

Analysts and election officials point to several overlapping reasons, not one cause: years of national criticism of mail voting, Ohio's elimination of the grace period so mail ballots must now arrive by Election Day to count, and voter worries about postal delivery. The League of Women Voters of Ohio stresses that absentee voting remains secure, with bipartisan teams verifying identity before a ballot is mailed and again when it is returned, and advises anyone concerned to return a ballot directly to their county board or drop box.

So far, seniors account for more than half of ballots cast, and Democrats and unaffiliated voters lead Republicans in ballots returned. Whether the in-person surge means higher overall turnout or simply the same voters choosing a different method will not be clear until Nov. 3 — watch weekend early-vote lines in Cuyahoga County and the final-week totals.

items.title: University Hospitals systems remain offline heading into the weekend after 'unusual activity'
items.summary:
University Hospitals disconnected its systems from the internet after detecting unusual activity on its servers on Oct. 22, and as of Oct. 23 reporting there was still no timeline for full restoration. The precautionary shutdown took the MyChart patient portal and parts of the public website offline, and UH said it anticipated digital service disruptions could continue for the next few days — which runs through this weekend.

UH says there is currently no impact to patient care delivery, and it activated its response protocols and is working with outside experts to determine the scope and impact on hospital and ambulatory operations. The system's website carried a banner warning that only limited services were available. Patients with questions about test results or appointments were directed to contact their provider's office directly, and to call 866-844-2273 to schedule appointments.

UH has not said whether the unusual activity was a cyberattack, and it has not said whether any patient data was exposed. Those two unanswered questions are the core of the story for a system with 18 hospitals that moved 5.6 million patient records onto Epic in a roughly $400 million transition completed in 2023.

For patients, the practical guidance is unchanged until UH says otherwise: use the phone instead of MyChart, and expect delays reaching results and scheduling online. Watch for a restoration notice from UH and for any statement clarifying what the activity was.

items.title: Guardians' October run ended two wins short — now the question is urgency around José Ramírez
items.summary:
In a post-mortem published today, Oct. 24, Just Baseball looks back at a Guardians season that very nearly reached the World Series. Cleveland stormed back from an 0-2 deficit against Chicago in the ALDS, stole Game 1 of the ALCS in Tampa Bay behind home runs from Chase DeLauter and Patrick Bailey and a clutch José Ramírez single, then took Game 3 at home behind Gavin Williams to stand two wins from the Fall Classic.

The turn came after rain postponed Game 4. A seventh-inning defensive breakdown, highlighted by a DeLauter error that let two runs score, helped Tampa Bay even the series, Drew Rasmussen shut Cleveland down over seven innings of one-run ball in Game 5, and a spent pitching staff could not hold Game 6 back in Tampa Bay. The Rays won the series 4-2 — which is why Tampa Bay, not Cleveland, is playing Milwaukee in the World Series tonight.

The piece argues the young core is real: DeLauter posted a 139 wRC+ across 11 postseason games and 3.5 fWAR in the regular season, Williams struck out batters at an extraordinary rate in October and is under team control through 2029, and more prospects are close behind. Ramírez, meanwhile, posted a 152 wRC+ in the postseason despite battling injuries including a fractured hamate bone that required surgery — and he is entering his mid-30s while Steven Kwan enters his final season of team control.

That tension frames Cleveland's winter: a patient, development-first club deciding whether to act more aggressively while its franchise player is still at his peak, with baseball's labor agreement expiring in December adding uncertainty. Watch for the Guardians' first offseason moves and for any signal they will trade from their young depth to add an established bat.

baby.tip: Car seat week: install the base in the Acura now, while there's no rush, and practice clicking the Aria in and out and adjusting the harness a few times. If you want a second set of eyes, many local fire departments and hospitals offer free car seat checks — worth booking before the baby arrives, and anything you are unsure about is a good question for your OB's office or the pediatrician's office.
baby.fact: A newborn's stomach is tiny — about the size of a cherry on day one, holding only a teaspoon or so at a time, and it grows to about the size of an egg by the end of the first month. That's why newborns feed so often in small amounts at first: frequent feeding is the design, not a problem.
baby.fun: Tiny mission for today: build the 'first ride home' playlist together — one song pick each from Mike, Kelly, and the grandparents. Save it on both phones so it's ready for the drive home from the hospital, whatever day that turns out to be.
